---
engine: markdown
title: Add Transaction History
description: Predict dispute outcomes for transactions using shared account context.
---

The [first model](../getting-started.qmd) reads one flat payment. Now move that
payment into a `trxns` list and prepend earlier transactions from the same
account. Each listed transaction has its own dispute target.

The business question becomes more specific: which transactions in the account
will receive a dispute report after review? Visits to the same merchant, changes in
amount, and booking-time patterns can provide context. An **event
history** preserves those observations so the model can learn their
relationships. Compare it with your existing aggregate features to find out
whether that detail improves dispute prediction.

The latest payment appears once, at the end of the same list as the earlier
events. Its amount and merchant need no separate root fields.

## Add A Collection To Each Record

Your application supplies `trxns` in oldest-to-newest order, ending at the
payment being assessed:

```yaml
trxns:
  - booked_at: "2026-05-21T10:00:00"
    amount: 32.00
    merchant: Station Cafe
    disputed: false
  - booked_at: "2026-05-27T18:15:00"
    amount: 56.20
    merchant: North Market
    disputed: true
  - booked_at: "2026-05-28T14:30:00"
    amount: 84.50
    merchant: North Market
    disputed: false
```

Use one account review cutoff: here, immediately after the last listed booking
on May 28. For every transaction, `disputed` means a new dispute reported in the
30 days after that same cutoff. The full listed sequence is therefore available
context for every prediction. Attach the Boolean labels after that window has
completed; keep later events out of the inputs.

Order describes which transaction came first. `booked_at` supplies a timestamp
whose selected calendar parts can reveal recurring patterns. Those calendar
cycles do not represent an exact elapsed-time gap.

A fixed feature table might retain total spend and transaction count. Here,
the amount and merchant stay paired within each event: a cafe payment and a
visit to North Market remain distinguishable. This gives the model evidence
for learning account behavior without deciding every summary in advance.

## Describe The Collection With A Branch

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.xs(
    trxns=rf.Branch(
        length=32,
        overflow="tail",
        booked_at=rf.DateParts(
            dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"],
        ),
        amount=rf.Number,
        merchant=rf.Category,
        disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
    ),
)
```

`Branch` describes a collection of records with the same fields. This branch
keeps at most 32 transactions; `overflow="tail"` retains the last 32, including
the latest payment. `mask=True` hides every transaction's dispute label and
trains the model to predict it from the shared context.

## Use The Same Training Steps

Train this new model with the history present in each record. Your application
supplies Parquet files with the nested structure shown above:

```python
data = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    model=model,
    train="payments/train.parquet",
    validate="payments/validation.parquet",
)
model.fit(data, batch_size=128, max_epochs=20)
```

Prediction files keep the same transaction list and omit `disputed` from each
record:

```python
requests = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    model=model,
    predict="payments/requests.parquet",
)
predictions = model.predict(datamodule=requests, batch_size=256, devices=1)
```

In development output format 2, `predictions.trxns[i].disputed` contains the
answer for each transaction, with `inferred: true` on every record.

If your source uses different names or shapes, continue with
[Binding Data](../core-concepts/binding-data.qmd). To prepare these histories
from transaction tables, see [Preprocessing](../guides/preprocessors.qmd).

After preparing and evaluating this model,
[Learning From Event Histories](../guides/learning-from-event-data.qmd)
adds payment channels, account profile context, and a merchant-repeat target.
